_comment: Every checkable assertion on /rights/section-87, extracted so a tax professional can review the page in an afternoon instead of reading 1,600 words and inferring what is being claimed. This is the claims register: the same spine as src/data/figures/2026.json, extended from numbers to statements. `status` is the honest split — `sourced` means it was checked against the authority named and a practitioner is confirming rather than researching; `needs-practitioner` means it is a judgement call that only someone in practice should sign off. Nothing here is a substitute for that review; the page says so in its own words.
pageTitle: Do I pay tax if I work on reserve?

claims.claim: Section 87 of the Indian Act exempts from taxation the personal property of a Status Indian or a band situated on a reserve.
claims.authority: Indian Act, RSC 1985, c I-5, s. 87
claims.note: The page states the statute in plain language rather than quoting it.
claims.sourceQuote: personal property of an Indian or a band situated on a reserve.

claims.claim: The connecting-factors test for locating income comes from the Supreme Court of Canada's decision in Williams v. Canada.
claims.sourceNote: Citation verified by inspection of the Indian Act text and standard practice; the SCC and CanLII URLs could not be confirmed from this machine (one resolved to a different case, the other is bot-blocked). Link left off deliberately rather than guessed.

claims.claim: The connecting factors that matter for employment income include where the duties are performed, where the employer is located, who benefits from the work, and where the employee lives.
claims.authority: CRA — Indian Act Exemption for Employment Income Guidelines
claims.note: The page ranks these as 'the most important ones'. A practitioner should confirm the ranking, not just the list.

claims.claim: Living on reserve and working for the band office on reserve is likely fully exempt.
Living on reserve but commuting to a private employer in the city is likely not exempt; living on reserve alone is usually not enough.
Working for an on-reserve employer from a city office is a grey zone that depends on the specific facts.
claims.note: The page declines to give an answer here. Confirm that declining is correct rather than under-claiming.

claims.claim: A teacher at an on-reserve school is typically exempt.
For hybrid work split between home on reserve and an office off reserve, CRA may allow a partial exemption proportional to time worked on reserve, but this is not guaranteed and depends on the facts.
claims.note: HIGHEST PRIORITY. This is the newest and least settled area on the page, it is the situation most readers are now in, and the page advises keeping a work-schedule log on the strength of it. If any single claim needs a practitioner, it is this one.

claims.claim: Exempt employment income is reported in Box 71 of the T4 slip.
claims.authority: CRA — T4 slip, Box 71 (Indian (exempt income) – Employment)

claims.claim: An employer placing income in Box 71 does not guarantee CRA agrees, and an employer omitting it does not prevent the employee from claiming the exemption.
claims.note: Consequential: it tells a reader they may claim against their employer's own treatment.

claims.claim: Investment income — interest, dividends, capital gains — is generally not exempt unless the investment itself is situated on reserve.
An RRSP held at a major bank is typically not considered situated on reserve, even for someone who is Status and lives on reserve.
claims.note: The page introduces this section as 'where many people lose money they shouldn't', so the claim carries weight with the reader.

claims.claim: TFSA growth is already tax-free for everyone, so Section 87 is not needed for it.
